newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian official clarifies lumber export rules.
newsitem.headline: Canadian official clarifies lumber export rules.

text.p: A Canadian trade official said on Tuesday that lumber companies that have used up 98 percent of their softwood lumber export quotas for the first year of an agreement between Ottawa and Washington (ending March 31) will be given the same quota for the second year of the agreement.

Ronald McDonald, parliamentary secretary to International Trade Minister Art Eggleton, said companies who ship less than they are entitled to in the first year of the agreement, could give the remaining part of their quota back to the Canadian government, who would redistribute it among other shippers.

"The industry has been well aware that because this is the transition year ... that we allowed companies that were not able to use ... their quota, to turn it back in by December 31 and they would therefore protect that quota in next year's equasion," McDonald told Reuters.
He said the International Trade Department was constantly monitoring companies' exports and had made "very aggressive" efforts to notify companies that looked like they would not fulfil their quotas.
"There was a considerable amount of lumber that came back in and it has been redistributed," McDonald said.
McDonald was responding to questions following recent wide swings in the U.S. lumber futures market on speculation about Canadian lumber shipments to the United States.
Chicago lumber futures traded limit down Tuesday morning, partly on speculation that Canadian firms would boost exports to meet their allocations.
But McDonald said he did not expect a flurry of Canadian lumber to hit the market in the last quarter of the first year of the agreement.
"If there are companies that are still out there that have not fully utilized their quota, I'm not so worried about any dumping because I don't think it will take place," McDonald said.

"Most of these companies are dealing with contracts that they have negotiated in the last quarter that they fulfil in this quarter. And we know that there is very strong demand in the United States for Canadian softwood lumber."
He said he had information that the U.S. home building industry was very concerned that the current quota system for Canadian lumber shipments was driving retail home prices up.
"If anything, I think the U.S. government would like to see more Canadian lumber although they haven't told us that directly," McDonald said.
Under a five-year agreement between Canada and the United States, from April 1, Canadian lumber exports which exceed quarterly or annual quotas are subject to export fees.
Export quotas are allocated for each province on a company-by-company basis. Shippers who have not been given an allocation are subject to fees.

McDonald said that during the first year of the agreement shippers who do not fulfil their quotas can give the remainder back to the government for redistribution no matter how much of their quota they have left.

However, beginning with the second year of the agreement, only shippers who have fulfilled at least 90 percent of their allocation would be allowed to give back the rest and still get 100 percent of their quota for the following year.
Shippers must give back any extra lumber before the end of the third quarter of the respective year.
Those who ship less than 90 percent would have their quotas cut back by a maximum of 20 percent for the following year. ((Malina Poshtova Zang, Reuters Ottawa Bureau, 613-235-6745))
